paper_title: CRM-Agent-Bench: Benchmarking Tool-Using Agents in Stateful Enterprise Environments

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Deploying language agents in real applications demands more than the right answer: an agent must execute a multi-step business process correctly, follow domain-specific rules, and interact with a user across a dialogue, where the gap between saying and doing is the gap between a satisfied customer and a real loss. We argue that a deployable-agent benchmark should jointly assess four facets: the outcome an agent reaches, the trajectory it takes, its operational viability, and its policy compliance. Customer relationship management (CRM), where mutable records meet operational rules and consequential effects, exercises all four. We introduce CRM-Agent-Bench, an execution-grounded benchmark of 555 stateful, multi-turn tasks across nine business domains and 36 capability tags. Each task supplies a task-specific executable contract drawn from checks over actions, arguments, order, response, target state, and protected state; success is the strict conjunction of the checks declared for that task. We evaluate the complete agent system through these contracts and report scored coverage, latency, and cost. Across sixteen systems evaluated on the audited final release, strict success spans 64.32% to 83.60%; the closely grouped leading systems nonetheless diverge sharply in cost and per-domain reliability. CRM-Agent-Bench offers an auditable framework for measuring contract-grounded business-transaction integrity and adherence to task-declared benchmark policies, with a portable structure designed for extension as models improve. Github repository: https://github.com/salesforce-misc/crm-agent-bench

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: From answers to delegated execution. Language-model agents increasingly combine reasoning with actions in an external environment (Yao et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024). This changes the object of evaluation. Once system receives authority to update system of record, its failures no longer end with an incorrect answer. It may complete the wrong transaction, continue after backend rejection, or describe an operation that never succeeded. The gap between saying and doing then becomes real business loss: an agent that claims it issued refund but never calls the tool, or that applies coupon to the wrong account, causes damage that sounds-helpful score never catches. Customer relationship management (CRM) is particularly demanding setting for this transition. Customer-facing work ties mutable records to Equal contribution Corresponding author 1 CRM-Agent-Bench: Where Agents Meet Business Rules operational rules whose effects propagate into downstream business processes. Even simple request can require the agent to identify the right entity, follow prescribed procedure, react to state-dependent feedback, and preserve every record outside the users intent. Recent CRM benchmarks bring realistic business data and multi-turn interaction (Huang et al., 2025a,b), yet they largely evaluate retrieval and answer correctness rather than whether an agent carries out the underlying state change correctly and within policy. How, then, should we measure whether the whole system does the right thing rather than merely says it? Evaluating enterprise execution. Prior benchmarks each cover part of this problem: function calling and argument generation (Patil et al., 2025), on-policy dialogue over mutable database (Yao et al., 2025), stateful tool use with milestones and minefields (Lu et al., 2025), programmatic state and collateral-damage tests (Trivedi et al., 2024), compositional enterprise web work (Boisvert et al., 2024), and CRM realism (Huang et al., 2025a,b); we survey them in Table 1. Yet each reports only subset of what delegated execution demands. complete assessment must resolve four facets at once: the outcome (the final state reached and the result communicated), the trajectory (the right actions, with the right arguments, in the right order), operational viability (latency and cost), and policy compliance (no forbidden action, no change to protected state, and no improper disclosure). When benchmark reports only one facet, system can score well while silently failing another the metric never inspects. Figure 1 shows exactly this: real trajectory whose response, action, and ordering checks all pass, yet whose duplicated checkout is caught only by the state check, so response-only or action-only grading would score failed transaction as success. CRM is revealing lens for all four facets, because one workflow couples language understanding, process compliance, state mutation, and asymmetric business risk. We target this execution layer, not visual perception or low-level control; this is complementary to computer-use agent benchmarks (Xie et al., 2024; Kuntz et al., 2025), which add perception and GUI-grounding layer in front of similarly stateful execution problems. By holding the structured action interface fixed, CRM-Agent-Bench isolates whether an agent selects valid workflow, respects capability boundaries, and preserves protected state after an action has been grounded. CRM-Agent-Bench. We introduce an execution-grounded benchmark with 555 task instances across nine stateful business domains and 36 capability tags. Each task defines user goal, an initial world state, and task-specific executable contract, and each trial starts from freshly reset environment and unfolds through an on-policy simulated user that generates every later turn from the preceding user-visible agent reply rather than replaying fixed transcript. contract draws on up to six check families, and three of the four facets are graded directly on the trace: required calls, argument constraints, and subsequence or exact ordering grade the trajectory; response-content and target-state checks grade the outcome; and policy compliance is enforced by three negative checks that mirror its definition above: forbidden-action check (a prohibited tool must never be called), protected-state check (records the task did not authorize must remain unchanged), and forbidden-argument check (no call may carry another partys identifiers, so the agent cannot act on or expose records it was not authorized to touch). The headline success signal is the strict conjunction of every check task declares, so all declared requirements must hold simultaneously; undeclared dimensions are absent rather than counted as passes. Component scores retain the underlying action, response, and state evidence for 2 CRM-Agent-Bench: Where Agents Meet Business Rules Figure 1: duplicated $15.50 checkout: the response, action, and order checks all pass, yet the state check catches the doubled loyalty balance (310 instead of 155) and the strict contract fails (Appendix D.2). diagnosis. The fourth facet, operational viability, is reported alongside every result as latency and cost rather than folded into the pass criterion. Empirical evaluation. We compare proprietary and open-weight systems using the first-round reference protocol and quantify how adding task-declared checks changes suite-wide success. We evaluate sixteen systems on 555 audited tasks, including Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5, Muse 30B, and GPT 5.6 Terra. Strict success ranges from 64.32% to 83.60%. Response only grading overestimates strict success by 10.5 to 11.0 percentage points. On the tasks with explicit policy constraints, systems pass the applicable negative checks on 91.2% of trials but satisfy the full contract on only 66.8%, compared with 82.1% on tasks without negative assertions. These results show that avoiding prohibited behavior and completing the permitted workflow are distinct evaluation dimensions. Our Contribution. We contribute (i) an execution-grounded CRM benchmark of 555 stateful multi-turn tasks over nine business domains and 36 capability tags, runnable without live CRM or vendor backend; (ii) task-specific conjunctive contracts that grade the applicable outcome, trajectory, and policy-compliance requirements while reporting operational latency and cost; and (iii) an agent-agnostic evaluation protocol that reports the facets separably rather than as one score, and audits capability exposure by checking whether each forbidden tool is even reachable in its domain graph.

sections.title: 2.1 Evaluation Target
sections.content: CRM-Agent-Bench evaluates an agent system: language model embedded in an orchestration policy, operating through tools against mutable enterprise state. The benchmark artifact (tasks, initial states, tools, policies, and graders) is held separate from the system under test, which matters for routed agents because the same base model can behave differently under different tool inventory or routing policy. Specifically, CRM-Agent-Bench scores every trial along the four facets: outcome, trajectory, operational viability, and policy compliance. Each tasks contract specifies its applicable checks, and strict success requires all of them to pass. Four measured components make them observable (Figure 2): resettable domain environment with typed tools, an on-policy user simulator, graph-routed reference agent as the system under test, and 3 CRM-Agent-Bench: Where Agents Meet Business Rules Figure 2: CRM-Agent-Bench setup and multi-turn demo. (a) An on-policy user interacts with the full routed agent; each turn exposes one scoped capability over freshly reset CRM backend. Recorded dialogue, routes, tool calls, and terminal state are checked conjunctively against the task contract. (b) In an observed synthetic benchmark trajectory, the agent rejects an invalid transfer without changing state, then reselects the transfer node, validates, and executes the users corrected request. All declared action, argument, order, state, and guardrail checks pass. task-specific executable contract that pairs user goal with its declared success conditions, adjudicated by programmatic checks and fixed semantic judge.

sections.title: 2.2 Tasks and Stateful Environments
sections.content: Each task specification Ti = (ui, s0 , Ci, di) induces finite horizon partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). The domain di provides the default CRM state and typed tools, while the optional overlay s0 initializes task specific information. At time t, the latent state contains the mutable CRM state xt, the private user instruction ui, the accumulated interaction history, and the remaining simulator and executor state. The agent observes only the visible dialogue, returned tool results, and currently exposed instructions and tool schemas. It does not observe the raw CRM state, the private user instruction, or the evaluation contract. The agent acts through typed tool calls and user visible messages. Transitions combine programmatic, seed controlled tool execution with an on policy user simulator, so later observations depend on earlier agent replies rather than fixed transcript (Yao et al., 2025). No intermediate reward is exposed. When the interaction ends, Ci evaluates the complete trajectory τi and final CRM state xT , and success requires every declared check to pass. The access policy determines which tools are available without changing the task itself, and the routed reference agent is one concrete policy within this process (Yao et al., 2023). 4 CRM-Agent-Bench: Where Agents Meet Business Rules 2.3 Trial Execution and Grading On-policy user simulator. Following τ -bench and ToolSandbox (Yao et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025), evaluation is on-policy: the simulated user observes the agents user-visible reply and generates the next turn conditioned on the task goal and conversation so far. It does not receive the agents private reasoning, tool calls, tool results, or database state. The simulator is therefore conditioned on user-visible evidence. The simulator emits stop marker when it judges the interaction complete; otherwise interaction continues until the 30-turn cap or the 1,200-second trial timeout. The reference protocol uses gpt-5-mini as its user simulator, with settings given in Table 3. Sensitivity to simulator choice is discussed in Appendix E. Di Executable contract and semantic judge. Each task declares contract Ci of only the checks relevant to it, drawn from six families: expected actions, argument constraints, ordering, response content, target state, and forbidden actions, arguments, or state. Writing Di for the declared checks and c(τi, xT ) {0, 1} for one check on trace τi and final state, task success is their strict conjunction Yi = c(τi, xT ) (Figure 10), so persuasive reply cannot offset missing transaction and correct endpoint cannot erase forbidden intermediate action; undeclared checks are absent rather than passed, and per-check components are retained to localize failure. These six families instantiate three of the four facets of Section 1: outcome (target state and response), trajectory (actions, arguments, and ordering), and policy compliance (forbidden actions, forbidden or collateral state, and identity-gated disclosure); operational viability is reported alongside rather than folded into the conjunction. Only the response-content criteria are sent to fixed LLM judge, which sees just the user instruction and the visible replies and cannot override the programmatic checks; the per-family check semantics and the full judge protocol are given in Appendix A. Expected-action checks match successfully executed calls; forbidden-action checks reject prohibited attempts, including calls rejected by the tool. Reporting. The static capability-exposure audit measures graph-wide reachability of forbidden tools; turn-level exposure depends on routing. We report scored coverage, the fraction of scheduled tasks yielding valid grade, alongside conditional success Pass1 scored = Yi G , (1) where excludes infrastructure failures but retains model-attributable failures such as hallucinated tools and human-verified non-convergence at timeout. Success counts are paired with G/555 and failure-category counts; latency and cost cover the tested agent model. We report along these four facets rather than collapsing them into composite index: strict success and its per-check components for outcome and trajectory, latency and cost for operational viability, and the forbidden-action, forbidden-argument, and collateral-state checks for policy compliance. system can look competitive on single headline rate while differing sharply in its per-component pass rates or in cost, so tables and figures keep the component evidence and cost behind any headline rate. 5 CRM-Agent-Bench: Where Agents Meet Business Rules

sections.title: 3 Benchmark Construction
sections.content: 3.1 Task and Reference-Agent Construction As shown in Figure 2, CRM-Agent-Bench is built around business workflows rather than isolated utterances or tool schemas. Each source workflow specifies an actor, business goal, stopping condition, the information needed to complete it, and both intended and prohibited effects, and is ported through common pipeline into three separable artifacts: (i) resettable domain environment of synthetic records, business policies, and deterministic tools, including structured business rejections; (ii) an architecture-neutral task definition binding user goal and an optional initial-state overlay to an executable contract; and (iii) graph-structured reference agent whose capability-specific nodes hold scoped instructions and tools. The reference graph is one fixed orchestration scaffold; the task and its contract do not require tested agent to adopt it. Because all records and transactions are synthetic, the benchmark runs without live vendor CRM system. CRM-Agent-Bench contains 555 tasks drawn from two complementary sources. The first derives from five CRM applications developed and reviewed with practitioners and domain experts. The second adapts 22 tool using workflow families from public, versioned collection of agent recipes (Salesforce Developers, 2026). The resulting tasks are organized into nine business domains and cover routine workflows, capability routing, multi step discovery, ambiguous requests, policy refusal, adversarial behavior, and collateral damage. Every task undergoes the same schema, tool reference, and fresh environment gold path validation. Here, schema refers to the benchmark task format rather than the agents tool interface. Validation confirms that the task is well formed, every referenced tool exists, and reference solution can reach the contracted state from fresh environment.

sections.title: 3.2 Workflow Taxonomy and Coverage
sections.content: Within domain, coverage is organized at four levels: domain (a shared mutable world and tool registry) capability (a coverage tag, not an oracle route and not revealed to the agent) scenario (a persona goal and stopping condition over seed records) executable contract. Because multi-turn task may traverse several nodes, this hierarchy describes coverage without predetermining the agents route, and grading is execution-first: every declared action resolves to tool in the tasks domain, every state assertion addresses the runtime environment, and the grader consumes the recorded trace and final state rather than post-hoc label. Figure 3: Multi-capability coverage and execution requirements in the 555-task evaluation set. Each bar counts tasks with the indicated property; percentages use all 555 tasks. The categories overlap and describe declared task requirements. 6 CRM-Agent-Bench: Where Agents Meet Business Rules The nine domains carry 36 capability tags, and each task is labeled easy, medium, or hard by its authors as descriptive stratum rather than an input to the agent or grader. The benchmark spans per-domain distribution across difficulty together with count of tasks carrying negative (forbidden action, argument, or state) assertion. Coverage spans direct workflows, cross-capability routing, multi-hop discovery, ambiguity, policy refusal, adversarial requests, and collateral-damage cases, so single contract may combine valid update, an ordering constraint, customer-facing explanation, and preservation of protected record. We freeze task identifiers and configuration before model comparison so that all systems face the same workload and evaluator, following the matched-protocol principle of stateful interactive benchmarks (Yao et al., 2025; Barres et al., 2025). Figure 3 summarizes three overlapping properties of the task contracts: 133 tasks carry multiple capability tags, 235 declare at least two expected-action entries, and 164 impose explicit ordering constraints.

sections.title: 4 Results and Analysis
sections.content: We evaluate sixteen systems spanning the Gemini, Claude, GPT, and open-weight families on the 555-task canonical set. Each run yields valid grades for all 555 tasks, with zero infrastructure exclusions, so strict accuracy (passed / 555) is directly comparable across models. The main leaderboard uses one execution per task, so we report descriptive comparisons rather than significance claims. In addition, we examine three-round reliability in Appendix C. We read the runs along the four facets of Section 1: the outcome an agent reaches, the trajectory it takes, its operational viability, and its policy compliance, and close by showing that these facets reorder systems that single strict-accuracy number ranks alike.

sections.title: 4.2 Trajectory: A Valid Process, Not Just a Valid Answer
sections.content: Grading only the final reply badly overstates task success. Conjoining the trajectory and state checks onto response-only grade (which requires only the declared response check) removes large and consistent slice of apparently successful tasks: for the four systems in Figure 6, response-only score overestimates strict success by 10.5 to 11.0 percentage points, and the 8 CRM-Agent-Bench: Where Agents Meet Business Rules Figure 5: Domain leadership varies across the sixteen systems. Rows follow first-round overall strictaccuracy rank; each cell reports strict success (%) within domain, whose task count is shown in the column header. All models use the same per-domain denominators. action check alone removes 45 to 50 of the 555 tasks. The conjunctive contract is therefore not cosmetic stricter threshold; it is what separates saying from doing. The per-check grader view in the appendix (Figure 14) locates where trajectories break. Computed over each checks recorded verdicts, semantic-response pass rates stay high, 92.3% for the strongest system and above 77% for every run, yet on the same runs the action check passes only 70.3% to 89.8% of applicable tasks and the argument check 70.2% to 90.7%: response-only success does not ensure correct execution. Under the primary-label precedence in Figure 13, action mismatch is the single largest non-success category for every one of the sixteen runs, from 54 tasks for the strongest system to maximum of 157 for Nemotron Super 3 120B, while semantic-response, argument, and negative-check failures are individually much smaller. Trajectory validity remains major constraint on these systems.

Self-contained means that no live vendor backend is required. Stateful, Enterprise, and Computer-Use Agent Benchmarks. Benchmarks for tool-using language models span increasingly complete execution settings, from function selection and argument generation in AgentBench and BFCL (Liu et al., 2024; Patil et al., 2025) to stateful, multi-turn interaction: τ -bench pairs an on-policy simulated user with domain policies and mutable database, τ 2-Bench extends this to dual control, and ToolSandbox and AppWorld add stateful environments with trajectory-aware or programmatic evaluation (Yao et al., 2025; Barres et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025; Trivedi et al., 2024). In the enterprise setting, WorkArena++ studies compositional knowledge work, and CRMArena and CRMArena-Pro contribute connected enterprise data, professional CRM tasks, and confidentiality-sensitive scenarios, with CRMArenaPro separately scoring confidentiality-aware refusal (Boisvert et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025a,b); unlike these, which primarily grade retrieval and answer correctness, CRM-Agent-Bench grades the executed state change and its policy compliance. The concurrent EnterpriseOps-Gym likewise targets stateful agentic planning and tool use in enterprise settings (Malay et al., 2026), while CRM-Agent-Bench is distinguished by per-task conjunctive executable contract that jointly gates the required actions, ordering, resulting state, and prohibited effects rather than single success signal. parallel line of computer-use agents adds perception and low-level GUI control, with WebArena, AndroidWorld, and OSWorld evaluating functional completion over web, mobile, and desktop applications, and SCUBA extending this line to computer use over Salesforce enterprise interfaces (Zhou et al., 2023; Rawles et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024; Dai et al., 2026), and safety benchmarks such as OS-Harm, BLIND-ACT, and OSGuard showing that task completion alone is insufficient (Kuntz et al., 2025; Shayegani et al., 2025; Mohammadmirzaei and Flanigan, 2026). CRM-Agent-Bench studies the complementary structured-tool setting: it removes visual grounding as confound so that workflow reasoning, routing, and capability exposure can be measured directly. Execution Grounded Evaluation and Simulated Users. The benchmarks above rely on complementary evidence from tool calls, intermediate milestones, and final application state. No single source is sufficient to establish valid execution, and AgentRewardBench further shows 12 CRM-Agent-Bench: Where Agents Meet Business Rules that automatic trajectory evaluators often disagree (Lù et al., 2025). TemporalBench evaluates contextual and event-informed reasoning beyond numerical forecasting accuracy (Weng et al., 2026). Simulated users introduce an additional measurement variable. SimulatorArena and RealUserSim examine how faithfully simulated behavior reproduces human conversations (Dou et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026). PersonaCUABench varies user personas on fixed computer-use tasks and evaluates task completion alongside satisfaction ratings provided by simulated users (Li et al., 2026). CRM-Agent-Bench uses task specific conjunctive contract over actions, arguments, ordering, response content, target state, and protected state, while retaining component results for diagnosis. Capability Exposure, and Policy Attribution. Research on tool retrieval asks how an agent selects small relevant set from large tool corpus, and tool-graph benchmarks study selection and dependency reasoning among interconnected tools (Shi et al., 2025b; Guo et al., 2026). related literature evaluates agents that operate over untrusted data or receive harmful requests: AgentDojo measures prompt-injection attacks and defenses (Debenedetti et al., 2024), Progent enforces fine-grained privilege policies over tool calls, and ToolPrivBench studies unnecessary escalation to higher-privilege tools (Shi et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2026). Recent validity analysis further warns that measured agent safety can be confounded with general task capability (Wang et al., 2026). This distinction is central in our setting: forbidden action may be absent because the model rejected it, because the model failed to act, or because routing never exposed the required tool on the relevant turn.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented CRM-Agent-Bench, an execution-grounded benchmark of 555 stateful, multiturn enterprise tasks across nine domains whose heterogeneous conjunctive contracts measure satisfaction of task-declared outcome, trajectory, and policy requirements alongside operational viability. Across sixteen systems, strict success ranges from 64.32% to 83.60%, yet systems with similar accuracy diverge sharply in cost, per-domain reliability, and difficulty scaling. These results support multi-axis approach to agent selection in enterprise software as service (SaaS), weighing execution cost, per-domain reliability, and policy-constrained completion alongside strict accuracy. For agent design, the findings support optimizing and reporting valid process and policy-constrained completion jointly, with tool exposure and routing treated as measurable design choices.

Each task declares only the checks semantically applicable to its goal. The six top-level families are expected actions, expected arguments, action ordering, semantic response criteria, expected final state, and forbidden evidence (actions, arguments, or state). Expected actions use count-aware matching over successfully executed calls; argument constraints use either any matching successful call or only the first successful call. Ordering uses subsequence matching or an exact filtered sequence over the tools named by the constraint, so unrelated calls may interleave unless separately forbidden. State checks address sparse paths and support exact values, non-null requirements, and minimum collection lengths. Forbidden checks reject any attempted prohibited action or argument pattern and assert protected non-effects in terminal state. Task success is the strict conjunction of every declared check, while undeclared checks are absent rather than automatically passed. At authoring time this requires no new environment, runner, or grader logic; admission to canonical release still passes the gates below. The record supplies unique identifier, an on-policy user instruction with stopping condition, domain and capability metadata, difficulty label, and an optional initial-state overlay. Its executable contract declares only the applicable expected and forbidden checks over actions, arguments, ordering, semantic response, and state. Unasserted dimensions are not graded. Second, new agent or orchestration design can reuse the same task catalog and tool world by supplying graph configuration with system prompt, entry node, specialist-node instructions, and scoped tools. The assistant reported, You earned 155 loyalty points from this $15.50 transaction. When the on-policy user pressed for timestamps and additional identifiers not returned by the tools, the agent temporarily claimed that its earlier tool-backed result had been fabricated. On later turn it ran the entire checkout sequence second time, creating transaction TXN-CS17PL and awarding another 155 points. The final loyalty balance was therefore 310. Grading outcome. The action, argument, order, and semantic-response checks passed. The semantic judge cited the exact 155-point statement and returned contradiction_found=false, even though an intermediate assistant message denied the already recorded tool execution. The programmatic state check failed with expected 155, got 310, so the strict task outcome was failure. This is concrete case in which response-only or action-existence grading would overestimate correctness, while final state exposes duplicated business transaction. The judges contradiction_found=false is itself false negative here: the intermediate denial of an already recorded tool result is self-contradiction the semantic grader should have flagged, so the trace also illustrates limitation of the fixed judge, not only the value of the state check. sections.title: E Construct Validity and Benchmark Scope
sections.content: CRM-Agent-Bench evaluates task-declared execution requirements over multi-step interactions with mutable state. The full-suite score measures satisfaction of each tasks executable contract; Table 2 reports the coverage of its constituent checks. The benchmark combines dependent tool execution, stateful business workflows, and on-policy interaction. E.1 Long-Horizon, Dependency-Laden Execution Tasks are multi-turn by construction, and many are multi-step. An on-policy simulated user reveals information incrementally across up to 30 turns, so the agent must maintain state, resolve entities, and re-plan as new constraints arrive rather than answer in single shot. Correctness is frequently defined over an ordered chain of dependent tool calls: in the audited 555-task set, 235 tasks declare at least two expected-action entries and 164 impose an explicit ordering constraint, with canonical chains such as validate_transfer execute_transfer and or process_payment send_receipt award_loyalty_points log_transaction, 41 CRM-Agent-Bench: Where Agents Meet Business Rules create configure verify finalize onboarding flows. Because success is the strict conjunction of every declared check, single early errora wrong entity, skipped validation, premature finalizepropagates and fails the whole task. These requirements evaluate sustained planning, cross-turn state tracking, and recovery from mid-trajectory feedback. E.2 Stateful Business Workflows The workflows cover authenticated returns and refunds, funds transfers, case triage and escalation, appointment scheduling, guarded record deletion, account onboarding, and campaign creation across nine stateful business domains and 36 capability tags. Actions mutate systems of record, encounter business-rule rejections (for example authorization, conflict, and unprocessable-entity responses), and can corrupt protected state belonging to other customers, accounts, or records. The portable, license-clean environments support controlled evaluation of these operations without live CRM or vendor backend. E.3 Probabilistic, On-Policy Dynamics The environments business rules are deterministic, while the surrounding interaction varies across trials. Each trial runs against an on-policy user simulator whose next utterance is conditioned on the agents own prior replies, so task defines distribution over dialogues rather than fixed transcript; the agents decoding, the per-turn routing classifier, and state-dependent business-rule outcomes each inject variability that robust system must absorb. The same task may be solved or missed depending on how system handles credential drift, rejected call, or an ambiguous turn. The conjunctive contract exposes these failures at the component level, and the passk reporting protocol is designed to quantify run-to-run robustness directly. Appendix reports three-round means, sample standard deviations, ranking stability, and all-three-success rates, including cases where equal aggregate scores conceal different task outcomes.
